title: Impact of Low Energy Availability on Hormonal Balance, Athletic Performance and Psychological Well-being in Endurance Master Athletes
summary: This study examines how short-term differences in daily energy intake influence health and performance in well-trained endurance athletes aged 50 to 65 years. Each participant completes two separate 3-day phases. In one phase, daily energy intake is lower, and in the other phase, it is higher. During both phases, participants perform the same standardized running sessions. Before and after each phase, laboratory tests are conducted to measure physical performance, blood markers, metabolism, and psychological well-being. On testing days, participants receive a standardized breakfast before exercise testing. The aim is to understand how short-term differences in energy availability affect physiological responses and performance in older endurance athletes.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Master endurance athletes aged 50–65 years and competing in endurance disciplines (running or race walking)
Post-menopausal status for women, defined as the absence of menstruation for at least 12 months and confirmed by circulating progesterone and estradiol concentrations
Body mass index (BMI) between 18 and 30 kg∙m⁻²
Well-trained runner or race walker (classified as Tier 2–4 according to the established performance criteria (McKay et al., 2022))
Engaging in ≥4 endurance training sessions per week
A documented competition history in running or race-walking disciplines
Achieving an age-grade performance ≥70% in their primary athletic discipline, calculated according to World Masters Athletics Table
Stable body mass, defined as a change of no more than ±3 kg within the past 6 months
Willingness and ability to maintain habitual endurance training routines throughout the study period
Exclusion criteria:
Low Energy Availability (LEA) Risk Indicators
•	Eating Disorder Examination Questionnaire (EDE-Q) global score ≥ 2.3 for women, > 1.68 for men
•	Current or previous diagnosed eating disorder
•	Resting metabolic rate (RMR) ratio < 0.9, indicating potential metabolic suppression
Hormonal and Medical Factors
•	Use of hormonal contraception or hormone replacement therapy
•	Use of medications affecting hormonal, metabolic, or inflammatory markers
•	Diagnosed diabetes mellitus
Musculoskeletal and Health Factors
•	Lower body injuries that prevent participation in intense exercise testing or regular training
•	Current smoking
Weight Stability and Blood Donation
•	Unstable body weight, defined as weight change >3 kg within the past 6 months
Dietary and Communication Factors
•	Vegan diet that excludes all animal-derived products
•	Inability to read or understand English or German, which would preclude comprehension of study instructions and questionnaires
